A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TravelBench, with matching core tasks, tools and evaluation framework. Their text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v3 includes complete Appendices A–H.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of six LLMs on three TravelBench subsets, averaged over three runs (Table 3).

after.justification: v3 reports original model evaluations, human validation, stability experiments, framework controls and case studies in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: The benchmark-construction procedure is refined. v1 assigns single-turn status when all three assistant runs finish in one turn, and multi-turn otherwise. v3 uses six-run thresholds: at least four one-turn runs for single-turn, and none for multi-turn, excluding intermediate cases. The core sandbox, retrieval-based tool simulation and scoring components remain.

E1.justification: The three subtasks and five travel-intent domains are retained. v3 additionally evaluates agents with live tools alongside cached/simulated tools (Table 4), extending the tested environment conditions. Its new geographic and demographic descriptions do not establish an expansion to new domains or populations.

E2.justification: v3 retains the six original model comparators and substantially expands actual evaluations. Table 2 adds GPT-4.1, Kimi, DeepSeek, MiniMax and additional Qwen models; Appendix D and Table 10 add scored Ministral3, Gemma3 and Llama variants. These are evaluated comparisons, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: The scoring and meta-judge model changes from GPT-5.1 to Gemini-3-Flash-preview. Feasibility annotation changes from two-model to three-model consensus, the unsolvable subset changes from 103 to 100 instances, and the reported cache grows from approximately 100,000 to 200,000 responses. v3 also introduces live-tool, framework-control and human-validation protocols. These changes prevent treating updated scores as same-setting performance changes.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's main model comparison, v3 tests judge repeatability and human agreement, dataset-label validity, offline-versus-online fidelity, and dependence on the tool-use framework. It also validates tool-call count as a difficulty proxy and adds successful and failed trajectory case studies (Sections 5.4–5.5 and Appendices D–G).

E5.justification: v1 reports averages over three agent runs without dispersion. v3 retains that main repetition count but adds separate judge-repeat and end-to-end standard deviations (Tables 3 and 5). Appendix E adds three-annotator voting distributions, exact 95% binomial confidence intervals for label agreement, and judge–human versus human–human MAE reporting.

E6.justification: The main numerical results and rankings are replaced: v1 Table 3 reports GPT-5.1 leading overall at 68.89; v3 Table 2 reports Qwen-Plus leading at 76.29 and GPT-5.1 scoring 75.04. These use revised settings and do not establish performance gains. v3 additionally reports many model scores, tool-error rates, validation outcomes, stability results and dataset distributions.

T1.justification: The scoring equations retain the same rubric averaging, multiplicative meta-judge and tool-error factors, and three-subset aggregation. v3 changes normalization and makes instance indexing explicit without introducing a different mathematical construction. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs; the added clarifications are explanatory and empirical.

C1.justification: v3 refines the novelty claim toward dynamically eliciting implicit user preferences through dialogue, while retaining unsolvable requests. v1 emphasized being first to combine multi-turn dialogues and unsolvable requests. The central contribution remains a broad, real-world travel benchmark with a reproducible tool sandbox.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of meta-judge calibration, tool-error penalties, difficulty and benchmark practicality. Appendix D distinguishes planning failures from tool-formatting failures, qualifying comparisons across model families. New limitations explicitly address restricted tool coverage and judge-dependent score comparability; Appendix F clarifies that unsolvability concerns unavailable capabilities or information, not merely model difficulty.

D1.justification: v3 supplies extensive information absent from v1: data provenance and collection dates, instance fields, profile de-identification and synthetic attributes, detailed tool descriptions, tool-simulator identity, framework/parsing details, and full assistant, simulator and evaluation prompts. It also adds code/data access information. These substantially improve documentation without establishing that every newly disclosed detail represents a changed implementation.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to interactive preference benchmarks, multi-agent planners and adaptive planning. Table 1 adds FLEX-TRAVELPLANNER, TripTailor and COMPASS, and explicitly acknowledges earlier multi-turn benchmarks. Positioning consequently shifts toward implicit-preference elicitation and the combination of realistic data, broad tasks and tools.

P1.justification: v3 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work and results narrative. It merges the agent and agentic-RL discussions, separates evaluation into its own main section, and adds structured limitations, ethics and explanatory appendices. This is substantial rewriting and reorganization beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v3 adds a benchmark overview diagram, score and difficulty plots, dataset and cache distributions, validation tables, and boxed case studies and prompts. The main results table gains tool-error columns, and the benchmark comparison gains an implicit-preference column. The existing tool table moves to Appendix C. These substantially change visual presentation and organization.

improvement.justification: v1's reliability claims lacked direct validation and detailed reproduction materials. v3 addresses these central weaknesses through human checks, uncertainty reporting, live-tool and framework controls, broader comparisons, and full prompts and data documentation. Reporting flaws remain: Table 15's counts total 1,489 despite its stated 1,500 trajectories. That inconsistency weakens the meta-judge analysis, but the wider evidential and reproducibility gains establish a substantial overall improvement.
